title: Invariant-section orbit ringed spaces and local categorical factorization
statement: Let $X$ be a locally ringed space and let a group $G$ act on $X$ by locally ringed space automorphisms [def-weil-locally-ringed-space-morphism]. The group need not be finite. Give $Y=|X|/G$ the quotient topology, and let $q:|X|\to Y$ be the orbit projection. For open $T\subseteq Y$ put $\mathcal F(T)=\mathcal O_X(q^{-1}T)^G$, the subring of sections fixed by pullback under every group element, with inherited restrictions. Then $\mathcal F$ is a sheaf of rings, $q$ is open, and inclusion of invariant sections defines an invariant morphism of ringed spaces $q:(X,\mathcal O_X)\to(Y,\mathcal F)$. Every invariant morphism of ringed spaces $a:X\to Z$ factors uniquely through this morphism. If every stalk of $\mathcal F$ is local and the induced stalk maps $\mathcal F_{q(x)}\to\mathcal O_{X,x}$ are local for all $x$, then for every locally ringed space $Z$ and invariant locally ringed space morphism $a:X\to Z$, its unique factor $b:(Y,\mathcal F)\to Z$ is also a locally ringed space morphism. For every $G$-invariant open $W\subseteq X$, $q(W)$ is open, $q^{-1}q(W)=W$, and the orbit ringed space of $W$ is canonically the restriction $(q(W),\mathcal F|_{q(W)})$; all these factorization assertions hold on the restriction as well. If $X$ and $(Y,\mathcal F)$ are schemes [def-pc-scheme], these factorizations are consequently factorizations in schemes. No scheme representability of $(Y,\mathcal F)$ is asserted without the local chart hypotheses.

proof.text: For any subset $U\subseteq X$, two points have the same image under $q$ exactly when they are in one $G$-orbit, so $q^{-1}q(U)=\bigcup_{g\in G}gU$. Every $g$ is a homeomorphism, being an automorphism of locally ringed spaces [def-weil-locally-ringed-space-morphism]. Thus for open $U$ this union is open, and the definition of the quotient topology makes $q(U)$ open. In particular $q$ is an open continuous surjection. For invariant $W$, the same equality gives $q^{-1}q(W)=W$. No finiteness of $G$ is used.

source.place: Tag 08ZK, lemma-quotient, characterization (2); elementary orbit saturation calculation

proof.text: For open $T\subseteq Y$, each $g$ preserves $q^{-1}T$. Its pullback is a unital ring automorphism on $\mathcal O_X(q^{-1}T)$, so its common fixed elements form a subring, and restriction preserves fixed elements. Given a cover $T=\bigcup_iT_i$ and matching fixed sections $s_i$, the sheaf axiom for $\mathcal O_X$ glues them uniquely to $s$ on $q^{-1}T$. For every $g$, restriction of $g^*s$ to $q^{-1}T_i$ is $g^*s_i=s_i$; uniqueness of this gluing gives $g^*s=s$. Thus $s\in\mathcal F(T)$, and uniqueness in $\mathcal F$ follows from uniqueness in $\mathcal O_X$. This also covers the empty cover. Hence $\mathcal F$ is a sheaf of rings, as required for a ringed space [def-weil-locally-ringed-space-morphism].

source.place: Tags 006T, definition-sheaf; 0072, definition-sheaf-values-in-category; 0091, definition-ringed-space; direct gluing verification

proof.text: The inclusions $\mathcal F(T)\hookrightarrow\mathcal O_X(q^{-1}T)$ are unital ring maps commuting with restriction, hence, with the continuous map $q$, define a morphism of ringed spaces by [def-weil-locally-ringed-space-morphism]. For each $g$, its composite with $g:X\to X$ has the same base map since $qg=q$, and the same section maps since $g^*s=s$ for $s\in\mathcal F(T)$. Thus this ringed-space morphism is invariant.

Let $a:X\to Z$ be an invariant ringed-space morphism. Its continuous base map is constant on each orbit, so the rule $b(q(x))=a(x)$ defines a unique set map $b:Y\to|Z|$. For open $V\subseteq Z$, one has $q^{-1}(b^{-1}V)=a^{-1}V$, which is open by continuity of $a$. The quotient topology therefore makes $b^{-1}V$ open, proving continuity of $b$.

source.place: Tag 08ZK, lemma-quotient, characterization (2); ringed-space morphisms as defined in Stacks 0091

proof.text: For every open $V\subseteq Z$ and $t\in\mathcal O_Z(V)$, invariance of $a$ as a ringed-space morphism and the composition rule in [def-weil-locally-ringed-space-morphism] give $g^*(a^\sharp_V(t))=a^\sharp_V(t)$ for every $g$. Since $a^{-1}V=q^{-1}(b^{-1}V)$, define $b^\sharp_V(t)$ to be this same section, now in $\mathcal F(b^{-1}V)$. These maps are unital ring homomorphisms and commute with restriction because the maps $a^\sharp_V$ do. They make $b$ a ringed-space morphism, and their defining equality gives $b\circ q=a$ on base maps and on every section map.

If $c:(Y,\mathcal F)\to Z$ also satisfies $c\circ q=a$, surjectivity of $q$ gives $c=b$ on points. For each open $V\subseteq Z$, the composite of $c^\sharp_V$ with the inclusion $\mathcal F(b^{-1}V)\hookrightarrow\mathcal O_X(a^{-1}V)$ must be $a^\sharp_V$, just as for $b^\sharp_V$. Injectivity of this inclusion forces $c^\sharp_V=b^\sharp_V$. The definition of a ringed-space morphism [def-weil-locally-ringed-space-morphism] now gives equality of the morphisms, proving uniqueness.

source.place: Tags 0091, definition-ringed-space; 0093, definition-composition-maps-ringed-spaces; injectivity of the explicitly defined inclusions

proof.text: Assume the stated locality hypotheses and that $a$ is a locally ringed space morphism. Fix $y\in Y$ and choose $x$ with $q(x)=y$. Put $A=\mathcal O_{Z,b(y)}$, $B=\mathcal F_y$, $C=\mathcal O_{X,x}$, and write $\beta:A\to B$, $\gamma:B\to C$ for the stalk maps of $b,q$. On a germ represented by a section $t$ on $V\ni b(y)$, the formula in Step 5 identifies $\gamma\beta([t])$ with $a^\sharp_x([t])$, so $\gamma\beta=a^\sharp_x$. By locality of $q$, $\gamma^{-1}(\mathfrak m_C)$ contains $\mathfrak m_B$; it is a proper ideal because $\gamma(1)=1$, hence equals the maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_B$. Locality of $a$ gives $\gamma\beta(\mathfrak m_A)\subseteq\mathfrak m_C$, so $\beta(\mathfrak m_A)\subseteq\mathfrak m_B$. Thus $b$ is local on every stalk by [def-weil-locally-ringed-space-morphism].

source.place: Tag 01HB, definition-locally-ringed-space, clause (3); germ calculation using Sheaves 0078, section-stalks; elementary inverse-ideal calculation

proof.text: Let $W\subseteq X$ be invariant and open, and put $O=q(W)$. Step 1 shows $O$ open and $q^{-1}O=W$. The map $W/G\to O$, sending the orbit of $x$ to $q(x)$, is bijective. For $T\subseteq O$, its inverse image in $W$ is open in $W$ exactly when it is open in $X$, since $W$ is open; by the quotient topology this is equivalent to $T$ being open in $Y$, hence in $O$. Thus the bijection is a homeomorphism. For every open $T\subseteq O$, which is also open in $Y$, the invariant-section sheaf for $W$ is exactly $\mathcal O_W((q|_W)^{-1}T)^G=\mathcal O_X(q^{-1}T)^G=\mathcal F(T)$, with identical restrictions and quotient section maps. This identifies its ringed space with $(O,\mathcal F|_O)$. Steps 2--7 apply to this restricted action. In the local case the stalks and their maps agree with the original ones: intersecting neighbourhoods with the open subsets $O,W$ gives the same germ representatives and equality relation. Thus the locality hypotheses pass to the restriction.

source.place: Tag 00A1, definition-restriction; Tag 0078, section-stalks; explicit invariant-open identification

proof.text: Suppose $X$ and $(Y,\mathcal F)$ are schemes; then the locality hypotheses of Step 7 hold automatically. The stalks of $\mathcal F$ are local because a scheme is a locally ringed space [def-pc-scheme]. Let $s\in\mathcal F(T)$ and $x\in q^{-1}T$ with germ $s_x$ a unit of $\mathcal O_{X,x}$. Then $s$ has an inverse on an open $U\ni x$ inside $q^{-1}T$. For each $g$, applying $g^\sharp$ and using $g^*s=s$ shows that $s$ is invertible on $g^{-1}U$. By uniqueness of inverses, these inverses glue to an inverse $u$ of $s$ on the saturated open $q^{-1}q(U)=\bigcup_gg^{-1}U$, which is open by Step 1. Since $g^*u$ is also an inverse of $g^*s=s$, $g^*u=u$. Thus $s|_{q(U)}$ is a unit of $\mathcal F(q(U))$. So an element of $\mathcal F_{q(x)}$ whose image in $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is a unit is itself a unit, and the stalk map sends $\mathfrak m_{q(x)}$ into $\mathfrak m_x$, i.e. it is local. By Step 8 the same holds for the restriction to $W$. Hence $q$ is a morphism of locally ringed spaces, and Step 7 applies to every scheme $Z$ and every invariant scheme morphism $a:X\to Z$. A morphism of schemes is exactly a morphism of the underlying locally ringed spaces [def-weil-locally-ringed-space-morphism, def-pc-scheme]. So $q$, the factor $b$ and their restrictions to $W$ are morphisms of schemes, and the factorizations of Steps 5--8 are factorizations in schemes; uniqueness among scheme morphisms follows from Step 6. No affine chart or scheme representability has been constructed.
